• Texas Instruments has pushed ahead with large scale U.S. manufacturing expansion, including RFAB2 in Richardson, LFAB1 in Lehi, and SM1 in Sherman, while earnings estimates for the current year have been revised higher by 7.6% in the last 60 days.
  • The combination of long lived analog product demand and heavier near term depreciation from these new fabs is putting the spotlight on how effectively Texas Instruments can turn this buildout into sustainable cash generation rather than just headline capacity.

Texas Instruments Investment Narrative Recap

To own Texas Instruments, you need to believe its manufacturing focused moat in long lived analog chips can keep turning a very broad product catalog into steady cash generation, even as cycles shift. According to OLetourneau, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the real edge is cost efficient 300mm fabs and decades long product lifecycles. The key near term catalyst is how quickly those new U.S. plants move from heavy spend and depreciation into solid utilization, which the recent earnings estimate upgrades point toward without changing the basic execution test.

The biggest operational risk right now sits in the same place. Large new fabs mean higher fixed costs, so any period of softer demand or slower industrial and auto orders could pressure margins while the capacity ramps. Depreciation and capital intensity do not derail the Texas Instruments story on their own, but they can compress reported earnings for a while if volumes lag expectations, which matters for a stock already trading on a relatively full P/E.

The clearest tie between the current news flow and the long term story is the U.S. manufacturing buildout, especially RFAB2 in Richardson, LFAB1 in Lehi, and SM1 in Sherman. That build is what turns OLetourneau’s view of 300mm cost leadership into something you can track in real time through utilization, unit costs, and cash conversion. Recent estimate upgrades and analyst visits simply direct attention back to whether those sites come online at the cost and yield levels management is targeting.

These facilities also intersect directly with income oriented investors watching Texas Instruments for its dividend and cash returns. Higher capex and depreciation compete with shareholder payouts if free cash flow tightens, so the ramp profile of RFAB2, LFAB1, and SM1 effectively acts as both a catalyst and a risk. If execution stays on plan, the expanded in house production can reinforce pricing on those long lived analog SKUs. If ramp timing or demand proves weaker, the heavier asset base can weigh on reported profitability for longer than the recent estimate revisions imply.

On OLetourneau’s numbers, that US$284.32 fair value for Texas Instruments lines up with a model that assumes revenue expanding at 14.2% a year and future profit margin settling at 30.0%, which effectively prices in strong analog demand flowing through those newer 300mm fabs.

Before this news, the most cautious group still pencilled in revenue of about US$29.5b and earnings of US$11.6b by 2029, yet viewed that as too rich for today’s price. Although the purchase is not a big one, by either a percentage standpoint or absolute value, it can be seen as a good sign.

That means that an insider was happy to buy shares at around the current price of AU$6.64. That means they have been optimistic about the company in the past, though they may have changed their mind. data.title: What Has Changed For XPeng Since Its 59% Fall
data.description:
XPeng has just rolled out what it calls China’s first mass-produced Robotaxi built on in-house Level 4 autonomous tech, a headline-grabbing step in its Physical AI push. Investors who held XPeng over the past year are down 58.8%, including dividends. That result reflects every hope and worry baked in since late 2025. If you had been weighing a position back then, how should this Robotaxi milestone reshape what you expect from the core auto business and margins now?

The useful thing about a Narrative is that the reasoning is checkable: the assumptions sit beside the argument, and together they imply an estimated Fair Value you can disagree with.

This theme extends beyond XPeng. See which of 94 robotics and automation stocks may still merit a closer look.

What XPeng Investors Were Really Arguing About

The shares cost US$20.79 at the start of the period. Anyone looking at XPeng then had to choose between two very different stories about what that price already assumed.

The bullish narrative saw Fair Value at US$26.29, based on XPeng using international expansion and partnerships to support revenue growth of 31.6% a year and a future profit margin of 4.6%.

The bearish view put Fair Value at US$18.06 and focused on global EV rivalry. This narrative highlighted pricing pressure, regulatory risks around tariffs, and rising compliance costs as threats to margins and cash generation.

What The Evidence Did To The XPeng Argument

XPeng’s launch of a mass-produced Level 4 Robotaxi using in-house hardware and software backed the bullish idea that proprietary tech and Physical AI could matter for pricing power and new revenue streams. The same window showed a tougher reality on the income statement. Revenue in Q3 2026 was CNY 24,276.0m, yet net margin fell from a 1.9% loss to a 3.6% loss. Overall, the evidence cut both ways.

The key lesson is simple. When a story leans on premium tech and new platforms, track whether net margin is actually moving toward profit alongside product milestones, not just whether XPeng or any peer is shipping more units.

What XPeng’s Lower Price Is Asking You To Believe

XPeng trades at US$8.99, so the stock is well below where earlier bulls were arguing, but the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St still places its Fair Value above that level.

The Narrative leans on Physical AI, Robotaxi and overseas EVs sharing one tech stack. That higher figure assumes XPeng eventually turns that shared platform into meaningfully stronger margins.

"XPeng's shift from a pure EV maker to a broader Physical AI group that reuses its in-house chips, models and software across vehicles, Robotaxi and humanoid robots is expected to create multiple revenue streams from a single technology stack and improve long term returns on R&D investment."

An XPeng Check One Step Away

XPeng talks about Physical AI and robots moving beyond cars. Another player is chasing that idea from a different angle.

Where XPeng leans on Robotaxi fleets, this other business is pushing humanoid machines as a labour platform. The pitch is simple and software driven.

Sell the robot once, then sell new skills over time. Each software upgrade turns a one-off hardware sale into a repeat service relationship.

That echoes how recurring digital fees changed what a smartphone really was. It turned devices into evolving service hubs instead of static tools.

If XPeng executes on its own platform vision, your reference point might not be old auto makers anymore. It could be whoever turns physical work into a software subscription.
